objective: Define broken access control and separate it from the other failure categories it is confused with.

original.hint: All four describe real security failures. Which one is specifically about permissions being wrong?
original.question: A "broken access control" bug is when:
options: Users can access resources/actions they shouldn’t be allowed to
original.explanation: Broken access control means the server lets an identity perform an action or read data outside its permissions: changing an id in a URL, calling an endpoint the UI merely hides, or setting a field the role may not set. It is A01 in the OWASP Top 10:2025, the same position it held in 2021. Weak passwords are an authentication failure, TLS misconfiguration is a cryptographic or configuration failure, and missing logs are a detection failure - each is its own category.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Retain the authorization objective with a concrete unauthorized read. Remove unnecessary time-sensitive category rankings and avoid treating authentication as authorization.
evidence: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/

objective: Choose the correct storage form for passwords: a salted, slow password hashing function.

original.hint: The store has to survive being copied. Which form is still useless to whoever copied it?
original.question: Passwords should be stored:
options: As salted hashes using a slow password-hashing algorithm
original.explanation: Store a verifier rather than the password: a salted, deliberately slow password hashing function. Current OWASP guidance names Argon2id as the first choice, scrypt where Argon2id is unavailable, PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-256 where FIPS-140 compliance is required, and bcrypt for legacy systems only. Encrypting under a shared key is reversible by design, so a single leaked key returns every password in plaintext - that is key management, not password storage. Plaintext and hard-coded credentials expose everything the moment the database or the repository leaks.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Replace the claim that stolen verifiers are useless with bounded offline-guessing resistance. Keep the ordinary sign-in scope explicit and avoid encoding an unnecessary full algorithm-policy matrix.
evidence: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html

objective: Define a salt: a unique per-password random value mixed in before hashing.

original.hint: Rainbow tables are computed once and reused against every database. Ask what would make one table useless here.
original.question: A "salt" is:
options: A unique random value added per password before hashing
original.explanation: A salt is a unique random value mixed into each password before hashing, so two users with the same password store different hashes and no single precomputed table covers both. It does not have to be secret and is normally stored next to the hash; a secret value held elsewhere is a pepper, not a salt. In practice Argon2id, scrypt and bcrypt generate and encode the salt themselves, so application code rarely handles it directly.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Distinguish salt from pepper and session credentials. Remove the blanket claim that named algorithms always generate salts themselves, and explicitly preserve the possibility of offline guessing.
evidence: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html

objective: Recognize that JWT header and payload are encoded, not encrypted, so nothing secret belongs in them.

original.hint: Paste the middle segment of a token into any decoder. Ask who needed a key to do that.
original.question: A common JWT pitfall is:
options: Putting sensitive data in the (base64url, readable) payload thinking it’s hidden
original.explanation: The header and payload are base64url-encoded, not encrypted: anyone who holds the token, intercepts it, or finds it in a log can decode the claims without any key. The signature protects integrity, not confidentiality - it detects tampering and hides nothing. Keep personal data and secrets out of the payload, or use an encrypted JWT (JWE) when the claims themselves must stay private. Verifying signatures, setting a short expiry and using HTTPS are all things to do, not pitfalls.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Scope the readable-payload warning to signed unencrypted tokens rather than every JWT. Replace the suggestion to paste tokens into decoders with an integrity-versus-confidentiality explanation; retain verification, audience and expiry requirements.
evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519#section-3
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725#section-3.1
